correctness.rationale: The full-weight objective is strictly convex because the Laplacian-plus-constant projector is positive definite on connected allocations and trace of its inverse is strictly convex along every nonzero symmetric matrix direction. Individual edge weights map injectively to Laplacian off-diagonals. This forces a unique optimizer respecting both edge orbits. The two positive eigenvalue families have respective multiplicities \(m\) and \(m-1\), reducing the budgeted objective to \(C+A_0y+B_0/y\) on \(y\ge N-2\). Derivative signs handle \(0<t<2\), equality, and \(t\ge2\). Algebra gives the exact weights, optimum, deletion benefit, and all limiting regimes. The standalone rational checker confirms matrix inverses, edge budgets, spectral formulas, competing feasible points, and threshold equalities for 66 cases, without substituting for the proof.

originality.rationale: The 2008 primary optimization paper presents the general unpriced convex network-design problem and equal-price complete-graph solution, but its inspected analytical examples and extensions do not give a perfect-matching price-orbit threshold. The 2016 complete-multipartite primary paper gives fixed unit-conductance Kirchhoff values, including the cocktail-party deletion endpoint, without optimizing the reinstated matching orbit under a relative price. The claim is restricted to the explicit two-price matching classification and its critical scaling; general spectral methods are acknowledged. Search results do not establish absolute novelty, and specialized earlier literature remains a residual risk.

value.rationale: A complete graph with distinguished paired links is a natural two-class reliability/network-pricing model. The exact price at which an entire sparse matching orbit should be pruned is a meaningful structural design cutoff; it is not a single ad hoc instance. The critical price approaches unity at rate inverse network size, producing an explicit nontrivial boundary layer in the optimizer and the resistance gain, and the macroscopic value has a second-derivative transition at unit price. These relations distinguish near-equal price design from fixed-price asymptotics, while not claiming a general-network theorem.
